source_policy: Primary lesson mechanics are grounded in the linked official Fortinet documentation. Community references are scenario/troubleshooting context only.

lessons.title: Upstream TLS re-encryption for HTTP virtual load-balancing VIPs

sections.title: Purpose and boundary
sections.html:
FortiOS 8.0 adds an upstream TLS leg for an HTTP-type server-load-balancing virtual IP. The feature addresses a common trust-boundary mismatch: a constrained client or legacy application can speak HTTP to a trusted-side VIP, while the selected real server is reached across an untrusted or shared network. With ssl-upstream enable, FortiGate accepts the HTTP request on the client-facing VIP and independently establishes TLS to the real server. This is reverse-proxy re-encryption, not end-to-end TLS. The client-to-FortiGate leg remains HTTP unless the client-facing service is separately configured for HTTPS.

The feature is specifically available when the VIP uses type server-load-balance and server-type http. It is not a generic switch that encrypts arbitrary TCP virtual servers. Treat the VIP as an HTTP proxy boundary with two independent transport sessions and two different security properties.

sections.title: Transaction and header mechanics
sections.html:
The client opens a TCP connection to the VIP listener and sends an HTTP request. FortiGate selects a real server from the configured pool, terminates the client-side HTTP transaction, then creates an upstream TLS session to that server. The HTTP request is carried inside the encrypted upstream session. The server's HTTP response returns inside TLS, is decrypted by FortiGate, and is then sent to the client over the original HTTP leg.

Because the two legs have different schemes, response headers can become semantically inconsistent. FortiOS exposes ssl-http-strip-secure-cookies to strip HTTPS-only attributes such as Secure, Partitioned, and SameSite=None from Set-Cookie headers before forwarding to an HTTP client. ssl-http-location-conversion can rewrite an HTTPS URL in a Location header to HTTP. FortiGate also removes HTTPS-only response headers such as HSTS and HPKP by default in this mode. These are compatibility transformations; they do not improve confidentiality on the client leg.

sections.title: Configuration pattern
sections.html:
Create an HTTP server-load-balance VIP, set the real-server listener to its HTTPS port, then enable upstream TLS and configure a compatible TLS version range. A production configuration should validate the real server's certificate and trust chain; the documentation's illustrative example disables certificate verification, which is not a safe default for an untrusted backend.

config firewall vip
 edit "web-vip"
  set type server-load-balance
  set server-type http
  set extip 203.0.113.20
  set extintf "wan1"
  set extport 80
  config realservers
   edit 1
    set ip 10.20.30.40
    set port 443
    set verify-cert enable
   next
  end
  set ssl-upstream enable
  set ssl-server-min-version tls-1.2
  set ssl-server-max-version tls-1.3
 next
end

If the real server requests mutual TLS, reference an appropriate client certificate with ssl-server-client-certificate. Review the VIP's certificate and cipher settings against the actual backend implementation. Attach the VIP to a firewall policy that permits the client-side service and inspect the selected real-server mapping separately from the policy match.

sections.title: Verification and evidence limits
sections.html:
Test the client-facing listener with curl -v http://VIP:80/. A successful HTTP status proves the client can reach the VIP and receive a response; it does not prove the backend leg is encrypted. Capture traffic on the FortiGate-to-real-server segment and verify a TLS handshake to the backend port, followed by encrypted application records. Correlate the timestamp and URI with real-server access logs. If the backend sees plaintext HTTP, the upstream option is not active for that VIP or the observed traffic is using another path.

Separate three failure classes: VIP/policy selection failure, TLS negotiation or certificate-validation failure, and HTTP response-rewrite incompatibility. A 404 may be generated by the backend after successful TLS; a TCP reset may occur before the HTTP transaction if the TLS handshake fails. Do not use an HTTP 200 alone as proof of upstream TLS, and do not infer backend certificate validation from the fact that TLS was negotiated.

sections.title: Operational caveats and troubleshooting
sections.html:
Upstream TLS adds cryptographic work and a second connection state per proxied transaction. Account for TLS handshake rate, session concurrency, backend certificate renewal, and HA session behavior when sizing the appliance. The feature does not encrypt client-to-VIP traffic, so use an HTTPS client listener when that first network segment is not trusted. Validate the backend certificate chain and name; avoid disabling verification merely to make a test pass. If the application emits HTTPS redirects or Secure cookies, decide explicitly whether to preserve those semantics or apply the documented response conversion controls.

In a realistic migration, a thin client cannot be upgraded to HTTPS but must reach a newly segmented backend. The VIP can preserve the client's HTTP contract while encrypting the server leg. Verification should include a packet capture on both sides of the FortiGate, a backend certificate check, and an application test that exercises redirects and session cookies. Record the client-side cleartext exposure as an accepted residual risk rather than describing the design as end-to-end encryption.

lessons.title: Central Firewall Users monitor: authentication-method and user-group filtering, VDOM identity, and session deauthentication

sections.title: Purpose and scope
sections.html:
FortiManager 8.0 adds a central Firewall Users monitor under Device Manager → Monitor → Firewall Users. It presents currently logged-in firewall users organized by managed FortiGate and gives an operator enough context to investigate identity-related access without opening each firewall individually. The monitor exposes the authentication method, user-group membership and VDOM context, and it supports filtering by method or group and deauthenticating a selected user.

This is an operational visibility and session-control feature. It is not an identity provider, an LDAP synchronization mechanism, or a persistent deny rule. The distinction matters during incident response: removing an active session is a point-in-time action. If the user still matches an authentication rule and policy, the user can authenticate again.

sections.title: How to interpret the monitor
sections.html:
The table is organized by FortiGate. The Method column and chart identify the authentication method used for the current firewall-user entry. The User Group column and chart show the group membership associated with that entry. Filters above the table narrow the displayed population by method and group. The VDOM column distinguishes entries that share the same username but exist in different virtual domains.

Use all three dimensions together. A username such as svc-build can exist in multiple VDOMs, authenticate through different methods, and have different group memberships. Filtering only on the username can lead an operator to terminate the wrong session. The device context is equally important because the same identity may be active on multiple managed firewalls.

sections.title: Session deauthentication workflow
sections.html:
Select the intended row and use Deauthenticate from the toolbar. The operation targets the active user session on the selected FortiGate/VDOM context. Confirm the device and VDOM before issuing the action, especially when a central operations team manages overlapping tenant usernames. The monitor is useful for quickly removing an established session after a credential leak, group change, or emergency access review.

Do not treat the action as a durable authorization change. It does not, by itself, disable the account in LDAP, remove the user from a remote group, change a firewall authentication rule, or create a deny policy. If the user immediately reappears, that is evidence that authentication remains possible, not necessarily that the deauthentication action failed. Investigate the source of identity and the rule that permits reauthentication.

sections.title: Evidence and troubleshooting
sections.html:
A visible row with a method, group and VDOM establishes that the monitor has a current user entry. A successful deauthentication followed by disappearance of that row is evidence that the selected session was removed. It does not prove that all sessions for the same username across other devices or VDOMs were removed. Re-check the table with the same filters and then with broader filters to identify additional sessions.

If a user is not visible, first determine whether the expected identity type is represented in the Firewall Users monitor and whether the correct device is managed and reachable. The monitor's documentation describes firewall users; do not assume every FSSO logon or proxy identity is surfaced identically. Use the FortiGate's own user monitor and authentication diagnostics to resolve an identity-source issue rather than interpreting an empty central table as proof that the account has no access.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A contractor's group membership is changed from VPN-Contractors to VPN-ReadOnly, but the contractor's existing session still carries the old authorization context. An operator filters by the old group, checks the FortiGate and VDOM, and deauthenticates the exact session. The user disappears, then attempts to reconnect. If the new session is still accepted with the old privileges, the next investigation is group synchronization and firewall policy evaluation—not repeated deauthentication. This turns the monitor into a reliable incident-response tool rather than a substitute for identity lifecycle management.

lessons.title: FortiMQ connector for ADOM-scoped indicator block/unblock propagation to FortiGate

sections.title: Purpose and architecture
sections.html:
FortiAnalyzer 8.0 introduces a built-in FortiMQ connector that can send blocked indicators directly to FortiGate devices. Earlier workflows commonly used a FortiManager connector to distribute block lists. FortiMQ provides an alternative when FortiManager is not deployed. It is not enough to click Block in FortiAnalyzer: the end-to-end path includes connector health, cloud delivery, FortiGate feed synchronization and a firewall policy or security profile that consumes the feed.

The connector is available in Fabric and FortiGate-type ADOMs and is disabled by default. Once enabled under Incidents & Alerts → Automation → Active Connectors, it automatically establishes a connection to the FortiMQ cloud service; there is no separate per-connector endpoint configuration. The connector status reflects API connectivity, not the enforcement state of every downstream FortiGate.

sections.title: Indicator transaction flow
sections.html:
FortiGate devices must send logs to FortiAnalyzer, both products must be registered under the same FortiCare account, and FortiGate must have Cloud-based Fabric Feed synchronization enabled. After those prerequisites are met, an operator can create or select an indicator in Incidents & Alerts → Indicators, from an incident, or from Log View. In FortiAnalyzer 8.0, Log View supports creating and blocking an indicator from an IP, URL, domain or MAC value.

When the operator confirms Block or Unblock, the block_indicator playbook runs in the background and sends the indicator to FortiMQ. FortiGate retrieves the indicator and updates its external feed. The feed can then be referenced by a firewall policy or security profile to deny the destination. The connector is ADOM-specific: the block applies only to FortiGate devices in the same ADOM. When both FortiManager and FortiMQ connectors are available, FortiMQ has priority; FortiManager is used only when FortiMQ is disabled.

sections.title: Configuration and control points
sections.html:
Start by validating the prerequisites rather than repeatedly clicking Block. Confirm that FortiGate logging is active, FortiCare registration is aligned, Cloud-based Fabric Feed synchronization is configured on the firewall, and the correct ADOM is selected. Enable the existing FortiMQ connector in Active Connectors. Because the connector is a built-in object, administrators cannot create a second connector or delete the existing one from the ADOM.

Next, create the policy-side consumer. The external feed must be referenced by the relevant firewall policy or security profile, with the intended action and policy order. A feed can be populated correctly while traffic remains allowed if no policy consumes it or a higher-priority rule permits the session. Conversely, a policy can be correctly configured but have no effect if the indicator was delivered to a different ADOM.

sections.title: Evidence and troubleshooting boundaries
sections.html:
Use separate evidence for each stage. A healthy connector status proves the FortiAnalyzer API connection to FortiMQ. The indicator appearing in the FortiGate external feed proves that the firewall retrieved it. A matching deny-policy log proves that traffic matched the consuming policy. A successful Block action in the GUI proves only that the request was accepted for automation; it does not prove delivery or enforcement.

If the indicator does not appear on FortiGate, check same-account registration, cloud feed synchronization and ADOM membership. If it appears but traffic is still allowed, inspect the policy/profile reference, rule order, address family and session state. Existing sessions may require separate handling depending on the policy change. If FortiManager is also enabled, verify that FortiMQ is active because it has connector priority.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: An analyst finds a malicious domain in Log View and selects Create indicator and block. The connector shows healthy, but the branch firewall continues to resolve the domain. The correct investigation is not to recreate the indicator: verify that the firewall is in the same ADOM, confirm the indicator has arrived in the external feed, and inspect the policy that consumes that feed. This stage-by-stage approach prevents a cloud-connector health check from being mistaken for proof of enforcement.

lessons.title: sFlow v5 packet and counter sampling from FortiSwitch ports, trunks and VLANs to external collectors

sections.title: Purpose and sampling model
sections.html:
sFlow provides network-wide traffic visibility without copying every packet. FortiSwitch implements sFlow version 5 and exports two kinds of evidence: flow samples containing truncated packet information and counter samples containing interface statistics. A switch-side sFlow agent samples traffic at configured interfaces and sends datagrams to one or more external collectors. The collector combines samples from many devices to show traffic sources, destinations and utilization trends.

This is statistical monitoring, not a packet-capture substitute. A sample rate of 512 means an average of one packet in 512 is selected; it does not mean every 512th packet is guaranteed to appear. Sampling reduces overhead but can miss short-lived or low-volume flows. Counter samples provide periodic interface totals and should not be confused with sampled packet records.

sections.title: Configuration objects and transaction flow
sections.html:
Configure the collector under config system sflow, using the collectors table to define an address and UDP port. FortiSwitch supports multiple collectors. The default collector port is UDP 6343. Then enable packet sampling on each interface to be monitored, set the sample rate and direction, and configure the counter polling interval. FortiSwitch supports trunks and VLANs as well as physical interfaces, but the exact interface/model capabilities should be checked against the feature matrix.

config system sflow
 config collectors
  edit collector1
   set ip 192.0.2.50
   set port 6343
  next
 end
end
config switch interface
 edit port20
  set packet-sampler enabled
  set packet-sample-rate 512
  set sflow-counter-interval 30
 next
end

The sample rate is model-dependent in its supported range; the guide documents a default of 512. The counter interval is in seconds and defaults to 30. Direction controls whether ingress, egress or both directions are sampled. Choose rates and intervals based on the visibility required and the capacity of the collector and network.

sections.title: Verification and evidence
sections.html:
Use get system sflow to inspect collector and global sFlow configuration, then inspect the interface configuration to confirm the sampler is enabled. Verify that the switch can reach the collector. A ping proves IP reachability only. Capture the export path with a filter such as udp port 6343 on the relevant interface or VLAN. Observed sFlow datagrams prove the switch is exporting; the collector's flow/counter tables prove that the collector is receiving and decoding them.

If no datagrams leave the switch, check the collector address/port, interface sampler state, sample rate, and whether an intervening firewall blocks UDP. If datagrams leave but the collector is empty, check the collector listener, source ACL and protocol version. A high sample rate increases detail but also increases export volume; an overly low sample rate can hide microbursts and short-lived conversations. Do not use sampled data to claim packet-level completeness.

sections.title: Operational scenario and troubleshooting
sections.html:
A network team sees interface counters in its NMS but no flow records. First confirm that counter polling and packet sampling are separate settings: a valid counter stream does not prove the packet sampler is enabled. Then inspect the interface's sampler and capture UDP 6343. A Fortinet Community troubleshooting article describes checking collector reachability, packet export and the sFlow process when data is absent; treat those checks as diagnostic context, not as the primary definition of sFlow.

At scale, distribute collectors, avoid enabling high-rate sampling on every access port without a capacity model, and document which VLANs/trunks are included. Sampling is valuable for trend and anomaly analysis, while targeted SPAN/sniffer captures remain the right tool when exact packet sequence, payload or lossless forensic evidence is required.

lessons.title: WIDS rogue-AP detection, radio scan duty cycle, accepted/rogue classification and MAC-adjacency tuning

sections.title: Purpose and components
sections.html:
Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS) monitors wireless traffic for intrusion patterns and records log messages when an attack is detected. Rogue-AP detection is related but distinct from frame-level attack signatures: it identifies access points observed over the air and helps an administrator decide whether they are authorized. The WIDS profile is configured on the controller and attached to a radio through a FortiAP profile. The radio can operate as a dedicated monitor or perform background scanning while serving clients.

Detected APs appear under Dashboard → WiFi → Rogue APs. The widget provides counts by detecting FortiAP, SSID and vendor. Operators can mark an AP as Accepted or Rogue and view offline or accepted devices. Rogue APs generate alert-level logs by default; unknown APs generate warning-level logs. If FortiAnalyzer is configured, detection logs are uploaded there for centralized review and compliance evidence.

sections.title: Radio scan mechanics and trade-offs
sections.html:
In background mode, a radio briefly switches from AP operation to monitoring mode. The documented default scan period starts every 300 seconds; each second, a different channel is monitored for 20 milliseconds until all channels in the band have been checked. This is not continuous full-band monitoring. Detection latency depends on the channel list, scan cadence and radio availability. Heavy AP traffic can cause packet loss when the radio leaves service mode to scan.

The ap-bgscan-idle control can delay the next monitoring switch until the radio has been idle for a specified period. This reduces the chance of dropping client traffic but can make scan completion slower during sustained load. A dedicated monitor radio provides more consistent scan availability where the hardware supports it, while consuming a radio resource that cannot simultaneously serve clients. Some FortiAP models also have dedicated-scan hardware; packet visibility limitations of the monitor radio must be considered.

sections.title: WIDS profiles and rogue classification
sections.html:
Create a WIDS profile under WiFi & Switch Controller → WIDS Profiles, enable the intrusion types required, and attach the profile to the relevant radio in the FortiAP profile. The WIDS profile can detect events such as spoofed deauthentication, association/authentication flooding, AP impersonation, AP spoofing, beacon flooding and wireless bridging. The rogue-AP monitor additionally compares observed wireless APs with the network's authorization state.

Rogue classification can use wired MAC adjacency. The global rogue-scan-mac-adjacency setting changes the maximum difference between the observed wireless AP MAC and its wired-side neighbor used in determining whether a suspect AP is a rogue. This is a topology-sensitive threshold. Raising it indiscriminately can create false associations; lowering it too far can prevent legitimate AP relationships from being recognized. Verify switch topology and AP uplink MAC learning before tuning it.

sections.title: Verification and evidence boundaries
sections.html:
Inspect the Rogue AP widget and table, then correlate the detection time with WIDS and wireless event logs. The presence of an entry proves that a radio observed an AP and the controller recorded it; it does not by itself prove that the AP is physically connected to the enterprise LAN. Use wired MAC tables and switch-port topology to establish adjacency. Conversely, no rogue entry does not prove that no rogue AP exists: the relevant channel may not yet have been scanned, the radio may be busy, the AP may be out of range, or the profile may not be applied.

If detection is delayed, compare scan channel coverage and the 300-second cadence with the event timeline, then inspect radio utilization and background-scan idle behavior. If traffic loss coincides with scanning, tune the idle delay or use a dedicated monitor where supported. If the AP is misclassified, validate the wired-side MAC adjacency before changing the global threshold.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A facilities team installs an unauthorized AP near a conference room. The AP is visible in the Rogue AP table but is classified as unknown rather than rogue. The correct investigation is to confirm that the serving radio's WIDS profile is active, inspect the AP's BSSID/SSID and detection timestamp, and then trace the AP's wired MAC adjacency through the access switch. If the AP is connected behind an unmanaged switch or a wireless bridge, the adjacency algorithm may not see the expected topology. The fix is to correct the topology/scan coverage or explicitly classify the device, not to assume that a missing wired neighbor makes the AP safe.

lessons.title: Rogue DHCP server detection using a dedicated interface, scheduled VLAN sweep and authorized-server/IP-helper inventory

sections.title: Purpose and design
sections.html:
Rogue DHCP Server Detection identifies unauthorized systems that answer DHCP requests on selected VLANs. FortiNAC uses a dedicated network interface and a scheduled verification task. The task moves the designated System DHCP Port through the configured VLAN list, observes active DHCP responders and compares them with the Authorized DHCP Servers group. A responder that does not match the authorized inventory triggers a Rogue Host DHCP Server or Rogue Device DHCP Server event, which can be mapped to alarms and notifications.

The feature is a scheduled discovery sweep, not continuous inline DHCP snooping. Only VLANs explicitly entered in the scan list are tested. The management interface eth0 is not available for this purpose. On a standalone FortiNAC server, eth1 is typically used for captive portal services, leaving eth2 as the likely scan interface. In a Control Server/Application Server design, an unused interface on the Control Server may be used.

sections.title: VLAN scan transaction
sections.html:
When the scheduled task runs, FortiNAC changes the VLAN on the switch port represented by the System DHCP Port group. During each VLAN change the port administrative state is taken down and brought back up after the new VLAN is applied. DHCP discovery traffic is then used to identify systems that serve addresses. The result is compared with the Authorized DHCP Servers group, and mismatches generate events.

This design has important physical and logical dependencies. The FortiNAC scan NIC must have an IP address from an unused subnet, and the switch port to which it is connected must be modeled in the System DHCP Ports group. Do not add the DHCP server's port or the management eth0 port. The VLAN list controls coverage: a VLAN omitted from the list is not scanned and cannot produce a detection event through this task.

sections.title: Configuration and IP-helper behavior
sections.html:
Configure the dedicated interface in the documented /bsc/siteConfiguration/vlanInterfaces file and follow the supported network restart procedure; changes to eth0/eth1 should be made through the Configuration Wizard. In the Rogue DHCP Server Detection settings, select the interface, populate Authorized DHCP Servers, add the System DHCP Port, enumerate VLAN IDs/names and configure the scheduled verification interval. For HA, both primary and secondary servers must use the same interface setting, and the corresponding ports must be present in the System DHCP Port group so monitoring continues after failover.

When IP Helper is used, FortiNAC may see the helper address as the apparent authorized DHCP server for each VLAN. The guide requires a Pingable model for each IP Helper address, including its MAC address, and placement of those models in the Authorized DHCP Servers group. If the IP/MAC pair is absent, a legitimate relayed DHCP response may be treated as unauthorized. This is an inventory-correlation requirement, not a DHCP relay failure.

sections.title: Evidence and troubleshooting
sections.html:
Check the task status, next scheduled time, selected VLAN list and System DHCP Port membership. Confirm the scan interface is up and attached to the intended switch port. When an event is generated, identify whether it is Rogue Host DHCP Server or Rogue Device DHCP Server and correlate the responder's MAC/IP with the authorized inventory. A clean event log is meaningful only for VLANs that were actually scanned.

If legitimate DHCP servers are flagged, inspect the IP-helper path and ensure each helper address is modeled with its MAC and placed in the Authorized DHCP Servers group. If no VLANs are scanned, verify the task schedule and the System DHCP Port group. If failover stops scanning, compare primary and secondary interface and port-group settings. Avoid treating an absent event as proof of a clean VLAN when the scan port was not attached or the VLAN was omitted.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A new branch adds a routed VLAN with an IP helper. The first scheduled scan reports the helper as a rogue DHCP server. The responder is legitimate, but FortiNAC compares the address and associated MAC against its Authorized DHCP Servers inventory. Create a Pingable model for the helper, enter the MAC, add it to the authorized group, and rerun the verification. This preserves the detection model while accounting for the routed DHCP topology. The Community technical note describes the same scheduled scan concept; the Administration Guide remains the primary source for current configuration and HA requirements.

lessons.title: SNMPv3 trap ingestion for host/user add-modify-remove lifecycle and directory enrichment

sections.title: Purpose and data model
sections.html:
FortiNAC-F can use SNMPv3 traps from external network devices to create, modify and remove host and user records. This lets an upstream system provide identity and endpoint information that FortiNAC would otherwise have to learn through separate polling or registration workflows. Trap fields can include host name, IP address, MAC address, operating system, role and an action code. The trap can represent a host alone or a host associated with a user.

This is different from using SNMP to query FortiNAC. The same SNMP settings page controls both outbound query responses and inbound SNMPv3 trap registration. Settings are global. If SNMPv3 is selected for trap ingestion, devices that query FortiNAC for information must also use SNMPv3; a mixed SNMPv1/v2c polling estate may need to be upgraded before enabling the feature.

sections.title: Trap sender and processing flow
sections.html:
The trap sender must be modeled in Inventory as a pingable device. Configure matching SNMPv3 parameters under System → Settings → System Communication → SNMP. The sender uses the FortiNAC management address and UDP port 161. In an HA deployment, send traps to both primary and secondary management addresses. In a FortiNAC Manager environment, model the sender on each server that must receive the records, unless host-copy settings make duplicate delivery unnecessary.

When a trap arrives, FortiNAC authenticates/decrypts the SNMPv3 message, parses the enterprise OID and varbinds, then performs the requested database action. The documentation identifies Add/Modify/Remove Host and Add/Modify/Remove User events. These events can be mapped to alarms. If a directory is modeled, FortiNAC checks the directory for the user and enriches the local record; if the user does not exist, it creates a record using only the data in the trap.

sections.title: OID semantics and record lifecycle
sections.html:
The example enterprise OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.16856.1.2.8. Host varbinds include name, IP, MAC and OS; role is a host attribute used by User/Host Profiles. The action field uses 1 for add and 2 for remove. The MAC address is required to remove a host. Adding an existing host modifies its record. If the trap includes user data and matches a rogue host, the rogue can become a registered host associated with that user.

User and host lifecycles are not identical. If a user is deleted based on a trap, associated hosts are not automatically deleted; they become registered devices. To remove those hosts, send a separate host-removal trap or delete them in Host View. If the same endpoint has two adapters with different MAC addresses, FortiNAC treats them as separate records rather than linking them as sibling adapters. Directory synchronization can also overwrite user fields according to attribute mappings.

sections.title: Verification and failure isolation
sections.html:
Capture UDP 161 to confirm the trap reaches the management interface. Because SNMPv3 traps are encrypted, a packet capture alone does not show the OID or varbinds; decrypt the capture in an SNMP-aware analyzer with the matching engine ID, username, authentication and privacy algorithms/keys. Then inspect the FortiNAC Event Log for Add/Modify/Remove Host/User and confirm the resulting record in Host/User View. Trap arrival does not prove the database mutation occurred.

If no event appears, verify sender modeling, destination address, global SNMP version, engine ID, security level and credentials. The Community troubleshooting article describes SNMPv3 MAC-notification traps ignored because of sender credential or trap configuration mismatches; use it as a diagnostic scenario, not as the primary feature definition. Also verify events are enabled and mapped to alarms. If only the primary server receives updates, confirm the secondary trap destination and Manager host-copy settings.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: An endpoint-management platform detects a laptop and sends a trap with hostname, IP, MAC, OS, role and a user identifier. FortiNAC creates the host and user records, queries LDAP for additional user attributes, and raises Add Host/Add User events. Later, a user is removed from the source system. The user-removal trap does not delete the associated host; the host becomes a registered device. A separate host-removal trap is needed if the organization intends to remove both objects. This distinction prevents a mistaken assumption that deleting a user automatically cleans up all endpoint records.

lessons.title: RADIUS EAP ECDH curve override for TLS handshake interoperability

sections.title: Purpose and EAP context
sections.html:
FortiAuthenticator 8.0 adds the diagnose authentication radius-eap-ecdh-curve control to override the default ECDH curve preference used for EAP. The documented default list is secp521r1:secp384r1:prime256v1. This is an interoperability control for the TLS portion of RADIUS EAP, not a replacement for certificate trust, user authorization or RADIUS client configuration.

EAP itself does not secure the conversation between supplicant and authentication server. Common enterprise methods wrap the authentication exchange in TLS, TTLS or another protected method. EAP-TLS provides mutual certificate authentication: the server proves its identity to the client and the client proves its identity to the server. A curve mismatch can therefore fail before the inner user or device authorization logic is reached.

sections.title: Where the curve fits in the handshake
sections.html:
The wireless or wired supplicant starts 802.1X with the access point or switch acting as the authenticator. The NAS relays EAP messages inside RADIUS to FortiAuthenticator. The selected EAP method establishes its TLS context, where the peers negotiate compatible cryptographic parameters, including the ECDH curve used for ephemeral key agreement. Only after the TLS channel is established can certificate validation and the method's inner authentication complete.

The curve override changes the ECDH curve preference for EAP. It does not change the subject key in a client certificate, the CA chain, the RADIUS shared secret, or the user's group membership. This distinction is important because a certificate using an unsupported public-key algorithm and a TLS handshake that cannot agree on an ephemeral ECDH curve are different failure classes and require different evidence.

sections.title: Configuration and dependencies
sections.html:
FortiAuthenticator's 8.0 release notes document the new CLI command and default curve list. Use diagnose authentication radius-eap-ecdh-curve to inspect or override the EAP curve preference using the syntax shown by the installed release's CLI help. The indexed Administration Guide documents the EAP methods and the certificate prerequisites: create or import a CA, issue a server certificate for FortiAuthenticator, configure the EAP server certificate and trusted/local CAs, configure the RADIUS client, and bind user certificates to user accounts when using EAP-TLS.

Do not blindly reduce the curve list to make one legacy client connect. First inventory the supported curves of the supplicant, NAS and server software. Keep the strongest mutually supported curve and verify the effect with one test client and one EAP method. The default list is ordered from secp521r1 to secp384r1 to prime256v1; changing that preference can affect compatibility and cryptographic strength.

sections.title: Verification and evidence boundaries
sections.html:
Capture the RADIUS/EAP exchange and inspect the TLS handshake stage. Correlate FortiAuthenticator RADIUS debug output with supplicant logs to determine whether failure occurs before TLS establishment, during certificate validation, or during inner authentication. A RADIUS Access-Reject is an outcome, not a root cause. A successful TLS handshake proves curve negotiation and server/client TLS progress; it does not prove that the user is authorized by the RADIUS policy.

Verify the EAP method, server certificate, trusted CA list, client certificate binding and RADIUS client definition independently. EAP-TTLS does not support challenge-based 2FA flows in FortiAuthenticator; the guide recommends password-plus-OTP concatenation for EAP-TTLS with 2FA. Do not confuse this method limitation with an ECDH curve negotiation failure.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A new laptop's supplicant supports P-384 but not P-521, while the RADIUS EAP server offers a curve preference that the client cannot negotiate. The connection fails before the user credential is evaluated. The engineer compares client/server TLS capabilities, uses the documented EAP curve override, and repeats the test while collecting both sides' logs. If TLS now completes but the user is rejected, the next investigation is certificate binding or RADIUS policy—not further curve changes.

lessons.title: RADIUS Message-Authenticator response validation and compatibility control

sections.title: Security purpose
sections.html:
FortiPAM 1.9 adds the RADIUS Message-Authenticator attribute to its requests and introduces a per-RADIUS-server require-message-authenticator option. The option is enabled by default, making response validation mandatory. This hardens the RADIUS exchange against packet manipulation and spoofing risks associated with CVE-2024-3596 (Blast-RADIUS). The setting is a protocol-integrity control, not a change to user credentials or group authorization.

RADIUS has a packet authenticator field, but that is not the same field as Message-Authenticator (Attribute 80). The Message-Authenticator is an HMAC-MD5 value calculated over the RADIUS packet using the shared secret. Both client and server must implement the attribute correctly and use the same shared secret. A mismatch or missing response attribute can cause FortiPAM to reject the authentication response.

sections.title: Request/response processing
sections.html:
FortiPAM sends an Access-Request to the configured RADIUS server and includes Message-Authenticator. The server validates the request, evaluates the user and policy, then returns Access-Accept or Access-Reject. When require-message-authenticator is enabled, FortiPAM validates the response's Message-Authenticator before accepting the result. If the RADIUS server does not include the attribute, FortiPAM can reject the response even when the server would otherwise authenticate the user.

The control is configured per RADIUS server object:

config user radius
 edit "corp-radius"
  set require-message-authenticator enable
 next
end

The documented default is enabled. Setting it to disable makes validation optional and is intended as a compatibility workaround when a server cannot provide the attribute. That fallback weakens the intended protection and should be temporary, scoped to the specific server and tracked for remediation.

sections.title: Interoperability and troubleshooting
sections.html:
Start with a packet capture at the FortiPAM/RADIUS boundary. Confirm that the Access-Request includes Attribute 80 and inspect the Access-Accept/Reject response for the same attribute. If the response is missing it, the server implementation or version is the likely issue. If the attribute is present but validation fails, check the shared secret, packet construction and HMAC calculation. Do not immediately disable validation because a generic connectivity test fails.

A Fortinet Community troubleshooting article documents a related case in which FortiPAM connects to FortiAuthenticator as a RADIUS server and the server rejects packets without Message-Authenticator. It recommends checking the server's detailed RADIUS debug and capturing the request. The article's FAC-side global client requirement is not the same setting as FortiPAM's per-server response validation; keep the direction of the RADIUS exchange clear when applying the diagnosis.

sections.title: Evidence and operational application
sections.html:
A successful RADIUS test proves that the configured test exchange completed; it does not prove that every user group or PAM policy grants the expected access. A capture showing Attribute 80 in the request proves FortiPAM emitted it. A valid Attribute 80 in the response proves the server returned a value that FortiPAM could validate. A server debug message about a missing attribute identifies a protocol compatibility problem, while a bad shared secret can produce a different validation failure.

During a server upgrade, stage the RADIUS change with one test account and retain packet captures before and after. Keep mandatory validation enabled on supported servers. If a legacy server must temporarily run without the attribute, document the exception, limit the affected server object, and set a deadline to upgrade or correct the server implementation. Do not disable the requirement globally when only one backend is incompatible.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: After FortiPAM 1.9 is deployed, a remote RADIUS server returns Access-Accept without Attribute 80. FortiPAM rejects the response even though the password is correct. The engineer captures the exchange, confirms the response lacks Attribute 80, and checks the server's support for Message-Authenticator. The safe resolution is to upgrade or configure the RADIUS server. Disabling the FortiPAM check is a temporary compatibility exception, not the preferred fix.

lessons.title: ClickHouse scheduled rule evaluation versus in-memory streaming and scheduled-via-SQL modes

sections.title: Why evaluation mode matters
sections.html:
FortiSIEM rules can evaluate incoming events in Streaming mode, on a Scheduled basis, or through Scheduled via SQL. The mode determines where and when the rule executes, how much history it can inspect, what evidence is retained with the incident, and which clear/exception controls are available. A rule that is logically correct can still behave unexpectedly when its evaluation mode does not match the required latency or query window.

Streaming rules evaluate incoming events in memory and are designed for real-time detection and high concurrent rule counts. Scheduled rules use disk access and do not scale comparably, but they can use complex analytic functions and inspect larger time intervals. Scheduled and Scheduled via SQL are available only when the deployment uses ClickHouse. Scheduled via SQL is additionally limited to Super/Global mode.

sections.title: Execution and incident lifecycle
sections.html:
When creating a rule, select the detection technology (for example Correlation, Correlation Using Lookup Table, Machine Learning or Profiling) and then choose the evaluation mode. Streaming evaluation processes the event stream as events arrive. Scheduled evaluation requires a query time window, schedule frequency and time-zone context; the rule runs against the configured historical window rather than waiting for each event to arrive at the in-memory evaluator.

Scheduled via SQL executes a SQL query on ClickHouse. It can be useful when the detection logic is expressed through supported analytic queries, but its incident evidence differs from Streaming. The documentation states that incidents from Scheduled via SQL do not show trigger events. It also limits each execution to a maximum of 100 incidents, supports only key attributes for exceptions, allows only time as the clear condition, and cannot be tested like a Streaming rule.

sections.title: Mode selection and constraints
sections.html:
Use Streaming when low detection latency and high concurrency matter and the rule can be evaluated incrementally. Use Scheduled when a larger query window or complex analytic function is required and the additional disk I/O is acceptable. Use Scheduled via SQL only when ClickHouse and Super/Global mode are available and the rule can operate without trigger-event detail. Do not select a scheduled mode merely because the rule is complex; model the time window, frequency, database and incident lifecycle first.

Scheduled rules require a query time window and schedule. Scheduled via SQL has stricter limitations. The 100-incident cap applies per execution; a large result set is not guaranteed to produce every possible incident in one run. If exceptions depend on non-key attributes or the workflow requires a non-time clear condition, Scheduled via SQL is not an equivalent replacement for Streaming.

sections.title: Verification and evidence
sections.html:
Verify the rule's configured mode, database type, query time window, schedule and time zone. Correlate the scheduled run time with incident creation timestamps. For Streaming, use the rule test facility and inspect trigger-event evidence. For Scheduled via SQL, the absence of trigger events is documented behavior, not necessarily a parser failure. Inspect the query results and incident metadata available for that mode instead.

Do not compare incident counts across modes without accounting for execution cadence and the 100-incident cap. A scheduled rule that runs every hour and a streaming rule that evaluates every event have different detection latency and aggregation semantics. When an incident does not appear, determine whether the event was in the scheduled query window, whether the job ran, whether the SQL result was capped, and whether the clear/exception logic suppressed it.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A SOC wants to detect a rare data-exfiltration pattern over a 24-hour window using complex aggregation. Streaming rules are too expensive for the desired window, so the engineer selects Scheduled on ClickHouse and configures the time window and run frequency. A second analytic is expressed as SQL and uses Scheduled via SQL, but the SOC must accept that the resulting incident will not include trigger events and that only key-attribute exceptions and time-based clearing are available. Those constraints are part of the design, not a validation defect.

lessons.title: Agent-based ZTNA destination ranges/CIDRs with port lists and port ranges

sections.title: Purpose and object model
sections.html:
FortiSASE agent-based ZTNA uses an application gateway and private-application objects. The gateway is the secure entry point, typically a FortiGate configured as a ZTNA application gateway. The private application object describes the internal resource by IP address, FQDN or wildcard FQDN. FortiSASE 26.1 Feature version adds IP range/CIDR destination types and port lists/ranges when the instance's default FortiClient for Windows version is 7.2.8 or later.

This changes the granularity of the destination object. Instead of creating one destination per server or one rule per port, an administrator can define a bounded range or subnet and an explicit port set. The object still has to be bound to a gateway and referenced by a connection rule in an endpoint profile. Creating the catalogue object alone does not grant access.

sections.title: Connection flow
sections.html:
First define the ZTNA application gateway with a unique name, the FortiGate IP/FQDN and the port designated for ZTNA. Then create a private application and select IP, FQDN, wildcard FQDN, IP range or CIDR. For a range, examples include 192.168.1.1-192.168.1.100 or 192.168.1.0/24. The port field can be Any, a single port, a list such as 80,443,8080, or a range such as 1000-2000. Select the application gateway that will proxy the traffic.

Next edit an endpoint profile, enable the ZTNA tab and create a connection rule that references the private application. The profile can also control whether traffic between FortiClient and the gateway is encrypted and whether SAML authentication uses the built-in FortiClient browser or an external browser. Those settings are separate from the destination address/port match. The ZTNA gateway acts as a reverse proxy and the policy at the gateway still determines whether the authenticated and compliant endpoint can access the internal application.

sections.title: Version and scale dependencies
sections.html:
IP range/CIDR and port-list/range controls are visible and supported for FortiClient for Windows 7.2.8 or later. The FortiSASE instance must be configured with a default FortiClient version that meets that requirement. If the UI does not show the controls, check the instance version and client baseline before assuming the feature is unavailable. FortiSASE supports up to 32,000 ZTNA connection rules, so broad use of per-application rules should be designed with the platform limit in mind.

During the scheduled monthly maintenance window, endpoint management and some ZTNA functionality may be intermittently inaccessible while the instance undergoes a rolling software upgrade. Plan changes and testing outside that window when possible. Existing agent-based ZTNA functionality can also conflict with other endpoint applications; if a profile previously enabled ZTNA and causes a client conflict, the documented control is to disable the ZTNA status in that profile.

sections.title: Verification and troubleshooting
sections.html:
Inspect the private application object for the correct type, address/range, port list/range and gateway. Then inspect the endpoint profile and confirm the connection rule references that exact application. On the endpoint, verify the installed FortiClient version and the assigned profile. At the gateway, verify the ZTNA listener and the identity/posture policy. A visible catalogue object does not prove the endpoint received the profile, and a matched destination does not prove authentication or posture authorization succeeded.

If one host in a subnet works but another does not, verify that the destination range includes the failing address and that the port is included. If the range controls are missing, verify FortiClient version 7.2.8+ and the instance's default client version. If SAML completes but the application fails, separate browser authentication from gateway reachability and policy enforcement.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A remote engineering team needs access to a cluster of internal management nodes over TCP 443 and 8443. The administrator defines one CIDR private application with a port list, binds it to the correct FortiGate gateway and adds it to the endpoint profile. The security team then verifies that only the intended endpoint group receives the profile and that the gateway's ZTNA policy still enforces user and posture conditions. This avoids a broad network tunnel while keeping destination and port scope explicit.

lessons.title: Hybrid priority/SLA strategy: SLA value, cost, link-quality and configuration-order selection

sections.title: Purpose and selection order
sections.html:
The hybrid strategy allows an SLA-mode SD-WAN service rule to combine SLA value and priority-style selection. It is not simply “best latency” or “lowest cost.” The documented selection order is: highest SLA value first; if several members have the same SLA value, compare administrative cost; if still tied, compare quality using the configured link-cost-factor; if still tied, use configuration order (cfg_order). Understanding this order is essential when multiple overlays are alive and in SLA but the chosen path is not the one with the lowest latency.

The feature also extends health-check evaluation with custom-profile as a link-cost-factor. A custom profile can combine packet loss, latency, jitter and reciprocal bidirectional bandwidth using weights. The resulting score is compared with a configured threshold to determine whether the custom SLA passes.

sections.title: Health-check and service-rule configuration
sections.html:
Configure the health check with the metrics and weights that reflect the application. The documented CLI exposes packet-loss-weight, latency-weight, jitter-weight and bandwidth-weight. The bandwidth term is based on reciprocal available bidirectional bandwidth, so a higher available bandwidth produces a lower penalty. Under the health-check SLA, select custom-profile-1 and define its pass threshold.

In the service rule, use set mode sla, set tie-break priority and the desired link-cost-factor. The tie-break option is configurable only for SLA-mode service rules. link-cost-threshold controls the percentage change in link-cost values that triggers policy-route regeneration; it is not the SLA pass threshold. Keep those two thresholds conceptually separate.

config system sdwan
 config health-check
  edit "hubs"
   set packet-loss-weight 1
   set latency-weight 1
   set jitter-weight 1
   set bandwidth-weight 0
   config sla
    edit 1
     set link-cost-factor custom-profile-1
     set custom-profile-threshold 60
    next
   end
  next
 end
 config service
  edit 1
   set mode sla
   set tie-break priority
   set link-cost-factor packet-loss
   set link-cost-threshold 10
   config sla
    edit "hubs"
     set id 1
    next
   end
  next
 end
end

sections.title: Interpreting the algorithm
sections.html:
First, SLA value represents the set of health-check SLA conditions passed by a member. Members with the highest value are preferred. Cost is considered only among members tied on SLA value. Link quality is considered only after SLA value and cost remain tied. Configuration order is the final deterministic tie-break. This means a member with slightly worse packet loss can still win if it has a higher SLA value or a lower administrative cost.

The Fortinet example uses multiple hub overlays grouped into PoPs. A preferred zone is selected based on the number of in-SLA members and a configured minimum-SLA-meet-members threshold. Within that zone, members with the same SLA value and cost are ranked by the chosen link-cost-factor. As metrics degrade, a member can remain alive but move out of SLA; if the preferred zone falls below the minimum number of in-SLA members, another zone can become preferred. Keep zone selection and member tie-break logic separate during troubleshooting.

sections.title: Verification and evidence
sections.html:
Use diagnose sys sdwan health-check to inspect each member's alive state, latency, jitter, packet loss, bandwidth, custom profile score and SLA map. This shows measurement and eligibility. Use diagnose sys sdwan service4 to inspect the service rule's mode, tie-break setting, member ordering, SLA value, cost, quality metric and selected interface. This shows the decision logic. A packet capture on the selected interface confirms actual forwarding.

A health-check pass alone does not prove that the member wins the service rule. If a path is alive but not selected, inspect SLA value, cost, link-cost-factor and cfg_order in that order. If the custom score is above threshold, the member may be out of SLA even if it is physically alive. If routes churn excessively, inspect link-cost-threshold rather than changing the custom-profile pass threshold.

sections.title: Operational scenario
sections.html: A spoke has six overlays across three hubs. All are initially alive and pass the SLA. The primary PoP is preferred because it has enough in-SLA members. Several members have equal SLA value and cost, so packet loss determines the winner. When one member's latency pushes its custom profile above threshold, its SLA map clears; when enough members in the preferred PoP fall out of SLA, the secondary PoP becomes preferred. The correct diagnosis requires both the health-check output and the service4 decision output, followed by a sniffer on the selected overlay.
